results.content: Increasingly, these tasks are assisted by numerical measures that rely on citation data to calibrate the abstract notion of scientific impact, including the h-index and number of papers in high Impact Factor journals (1). However,  suffers from two well-recognized biases (3–5): i) temporal bias, reflected by the higher rate of citations accumulated by later papers, an inflation process that makes it difficult to compare the impact of papers published decades apart; and ii) field bias, manifested by systematic differences of  across disciplines, creating the impression that papers in highly cited fields, like cell biology, have inherently bigger impact than, for example, mathematics papers, where citations are fewer. To further illustrate the advantage of , we compare it with two other popular indicators: total raw citations  and , which normalizes  with the average  of papers in the same year and field, as determined by journals (7). Despite these limitations, our proposal of a citation-based measure that is time invariant and free from discipline bias allows us to compare the impact of papers across years and disciplines.
